passage:
Dear Deepika,
Guess what, I'm basically the most popular girl in Class 10 now. I told everyone about Papa's new car (the big one, not the old one) and how we're going to Dubai in December. Everyone was SO jealous. Then I told them how I shouted at that senior who pushed Tanu in the canteen, and she ran away. Well, she walked away, but fast.
Now everyone knows not to mess with me.
It's funny, though. Tanu and Riddhi have been eating lunch in the library this week. They say it's for studying. And when I told the Dubai story again on Friday, Riddhi kind of rolled her eyes? I think she's just jealous.
Anyway, write back and tell me if you have anything this exciting!
Love,
Madhuri

qa.q: Where did Madhuri say the family was going in December?
qa.a: To Dubai.

qa.q: Why does Madhuri keep telling the Dubai and canteen stories?
qa.a: Madhuri wants to feel important and ranked higher, and enjoys making others jealous, perhaps out of a need to be admired.

qa.q: What could Madhuri notice in her own letter?
qa.a: That Tanu and Riddhi are eating in the library and Riddhi rolled her eyes, signs the boasting is pushing friends away rather than impressing them.

qa.q: How might Riddhi be feeling when she hears the Dubai story again?
qa.a: Riddhi seems tired and irritated rather than jealous, which is why she rolled her eyes and has been eating elsewhere.

grounding: Shows a teenager boasting about money and a fight to rise in the group, while missing the signs that friends are quietly distancing.

passage:
The results of the city hackathon came out on Saturday morning in Hyderabad. Madhuri's team had won first prize.
In the hostel mess, Aadhya from the next room was already on her third story about her own internship: the famous manager, the big project, the praise.
Madhuri waited until she finished. "Congrats on the internship. What's the project actually about?"
Aadhya blinked, then started explaining properly, and it turned out to be interesting.
Later someone asked Madhuri, "Didn't your team win something?"
"Yes, first prize. We built a tool for tracking water tanker deliveries. My teammate Farzana did the hardest part." Then she went back to her dal.
That evening Aadhya knocked on her door. "You didn't even post about it?"
Madhuri shrugged. "I told my parents. The tool works. That's the part I care about."

qa.q: What did Madhuri's team build?
qa.a: A tool for tracking water tanker deliveries.

qa.q: What does Madhuri's shrug about not posting suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Madhuri feels quietly proud and secure, needing no applause because the working tool is what matters.

qa.q: Which of Madhuri's habits show quiet confidence?
qa.a: Asking Aadhya about her project, sharing the win simply when asked, crediting Farzana, and not needing to post about it.

qa.q: How might Aadhya see Madhuri after that day?
qa.a: Aadhya seems puzzled and curious, knocking to ask about not posting, perhaps noticing a different way to carry success.

grounding: Shows a young woman who shares a win simply, credits others and asks about them, needing no applause for her achievement.

passage:
In the Pune office, Ankita had a way of turning every conversation back to her record. The award in 2022. The client who asked for her by name. The certification she'd finished in six weeks. At lunch the others traded glances.
Jeevan noticed something else. She did it most right after the manager talked over her in meetings, and her voice always sped up, as if she was afraid of being interrupted.
On Friday, after her presentation, he stopped by her desk. "The way you broke down the vendor costs on slide four was really clear. I'm going to steal that format."
Ankita looked startled. "Oh. Thanks." She didn't list anything else.
Over the next few weeks, Jeevan made a point of naming specific things she did well. He noticed she mentioned 2022 less and less. One day she even asked him about his project first.

qa.q: What did Jeevan praise about Ankita's presentation?
qa.a: The way she broke down the vendor costs on slide four.

qa.q: How did Jeevan feel about Ankita's listing of achievements, and why?
qa.a: Jeevan felt concern rather than irritation, reading the boasting as a hunger for reassurance, since it came right after being talked over in meetings.

qa.q: What approach did Jeevan use, and what changed?
qa.a: He gave kind, specific acknowledgement of real work, and over the following weeks Ankita mentioned past awards less and asked about others more.

qa.q: How might Ankita have felt when Jeevan praised slide four?
qa.a: Ankita was startled and quietly pleased, perhaps feeling truly seen for once, so she didn't need to list anything else.

grounding: Shows a colleague reading a peer's constant boasting as a need for reassurance and easing it with kind, specific acknowledgement.

qa.q: Why does Jeevan prefer to think Sameer is just jealous?

qa.q: What could Jeevan do to learn from this?
qa.a: Admit the joke was hurtful and tell Sameer so, instead of keeping a story where Sameer is the only problem.

qa.q: How might Sameer have felt on the trip?
qa.a: Sameer was likely hurt and humiliated by a joke about his dad's shop that everyone laughed at, and then left without a seat.

grounding: Shows a teenager insisting a lost friend was the only problem, a flattering story that eases guilt but blocks learning.

passage:
Hi Maria,
Exams start in nine days and I haven't opened the organic chemistry notes since August. Don't panic on my behalf! You know me, I work better under pressure. Last year I did the whole thermodynamics unit in two nights and passed.
I've been busy anyway: the dance club, the new series everyone's watching, reorganising my room (twice). The room looks great, honestly.
The funny thing is, every time I sit down with the notes, my chest goes tight and I suddenly need to check my phone. Probably just tired.
Actually, if I'm totally honest, which is easier in an email, last year's "pass" was by three marks. And I cried in the bathroom before the exam. So maybe "better under pressure" isn't the whole truth. Maybe I just don't want to find out I can't do it.
Call me this weekend? I might need a study buddy.
Vidya

qa.q: When do Vidya's exams start?
qa.a: Exams start in nine days.

qa.q: What does Vidya's tight chest when opening the notes suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Vidya is anxious and afraid of failing, which the 'better under pressure' story was covering up.

qa.q: What small step is Vidya taking by the end of the email?
qa.a: Admitting the real reason and asking Maria to be a study buddy this weekend, instead of waiting for the last two nights.

qa.q: How might Maria read this email?
qa.a: Maria might feel worried by the three-mark pass and the crying, and glad Vidya is finally asking for help.

grounding: Shows a student claiming to work better under pressure to avoid the real reason for not studying, a fear of failing.

passage:
The electricity bill arrived the same morning as the third reminder from the credit card company, and Siddharth put both, unopened, under the fruit bowl. Rent was due in four days. His salary was due in six.
It'll sort itself out, he told himself. Next month's bonus. Or the side project. He had been saying it since March.
His phone buzzed with an unknown number. He turned it face down.
At lunch his sister Sunaina called. "You sound tired. Everything okay?"
"All good. Just busy." He laughed. He always laughed.
That night he couldn't sleep. At 2 am he lifted the fruit bowl and looked at the envelopes, then put the bowl back on top. Opening them would mean knowing the number. Knowing the number would mean doing something.
He lay in the dark, heart racing, telling himself one more time that it would all work out.

qa.q: Where did Siddharth put the envelopes?
qa.a: Under the fruit bowl, unopened.

qa.q: Why did Siddharth put the fruit bowl back on the envelopes at 2 am?
qa.a: Siddharth felt frightened; opening them would mean knowing the number and having to act, which he wasn't ready for.

qa.q: What could Siddharth do instead of waiting for it to sort itself out?
qa.a: Open the envelopes in daylight, tell Sunaina the truth when she calls, and speak to a qualified debt adviser about the options.

qa.q: What would change if Sunaina knew what was under the fruit bowl?
qa.a: Sunaina could offer support and help him find proper advice, instead of hearing 'all good' while he lies awake.

grounding: Shows an adult with mounting bills telling himself it will sort itself out, because looking straight at it would demand action.

passage:
The bus was stuck in Gurgaon traffic for forty minutes, and Simran's phone was at six percent. She kept replaying her manager's words from the meeting: "Sloppy again." It was the fourth time this month.
It's me, she thought. I'm just not good enough. I should work weekends.
She messaged Vinita before the battery died. "He's right, I'm useless at this job."
Vinita replied fast: "If I told you my boss said 'sloppy' four times without ever saying what was wrong, what would you tell me?"
Simran stared at the screen. She'd tell Vinita to ask for specifics. She'd say one person's opinion isn't the whole truth. She'd ask whether the client had ever complained. The client hadn't. The client had sent a thank-you email on Monday.
The phone died. Simran sat in the dark bus, not happy, but steadier. Tomorrow she would ask her manager, calmly, which exact parts were sloppy. And she would read the thank-you email again.

qa.q: What did the client send on Monday?
qa.a: A thank-you email.

qa.q: How did Simran feel sitting in the dark bus after Vinita's question?
qa.a: Simran was not happy but felt steadier, having looked at the story with the kindness she'd give a friend.

qa.q: Which gentle questions helped Simran test the story?
qa.a: What she would tell a friend in the same place, what evidence goes against it, like the client's thanks, and what exactly was sloppy.

qa.q: How did Vinita help without arguing?
qa.a: Vinita didn't tell Simran she was wrong; she asked a question that let Simran see the story from outside.

grounding: Shows a woman testing a harsh story about herself by asking what she would tell a friend and what evidence would change her mind.

passage:
At the Onam gathering in their small town near Thrissur, Gopika clutched her new doll. Her cousin Parul was crying because she wanted a turn.
"I promise I'll share after lunch!" Gopika said, very seriously. Parul stopped crying.
After lunch, Parul held out her hands. Gopika hugged the doll tighter. "No. She's sleeping."
Parul's lip wobbled again.
Amma knelt beside Gopika. "You promised, remember? Promises are for later-you too." Gopika frowned, thinking hard about later-her. Then, slowly, she held out the doll for a short turn.

qa.q: When did Gopika promise to share the doll?
qa.a: After lunch.

qa.q: What did Gopika feel after lunch when Parul held out her hands?
qa.a: Gopika felt stubborn and possessive, hugging the doll tighter; the promise had felt real before lunch, but now she felt different.

qa.q: How did Amma help Gopika keep the promise?
qa.a: Amma knelt beside her and gently reminded her that promises are for later-you too, letting Gopika choose to give a short turn.

qa.q: How did Parul feel when Gopika said 'She's sleeping'?
qa.a: Parul's lip wobbled; she felt let down and close to tears again.

grounding: Shows a young child promising to share and meaning it fully, then finding the later self feels differently.

passage:
Payal had promised Aditi on Monday: "I'll come to your final, I swear." Aditi was the goalkeeper, and she was terrified.
On Saturday, Nandita's birthday invite came for the same afternoon, with a magic show. And it started to pour.
"Nobody will go to a match in this," Mummy said. "Go to the party."
Payal stood at the window, pulled in two. But she kept seeing Aditi's face on Monday.
"I promised," she said. "Can you drop me at the ground?"
Mummy looked at her for a long moment and fetched the umbrella.
Payal stood on the muddy sideline for the whole match. Aditi saved two goals. At the end she ran over, soaked, and hugged Payal so hard they nearly fell.
"You came!"
Payal missed the magic show. She didn't mind as much as she had expected.

qa.q: What position did Aditi play?
qa.a: Aditi was the goalkeeper.

qa.q: How did Payal feel standing at the window?
qa.a: Payal felt pulled in two, tempted by the magic show and the easy excuse of rain, but uneasy about breaking her word.

qa.q: What did keeping the promise teach Payal?
qa.a: That her word counts even when it is hard, and that being reliable felt good and meant a lot to Aditi.

qa.q: What did it mean to Aditi that Payal came?
qa.a: Aditi, who had been terrified, felt so happy and supported that she ran over and hugged Payal in the rain.

grounding: Shows a child keeping a promise to a friend through rain and a tempting party, learning that her word binds her.

subtype: Being let down by a broken promise [Receiver]
passage:
Debate coach's note, Friday. Noor
Dhruv (Class 9) won the inter-school debate final today. When the results were read out, he looked straight at the empty seat in the second row that he had saved with his bag.
His father had promised to come. On Monday Dhruv told me, "He's definitely coming this time." This is the third event this year that he has missed.
Afterwards Dhruv shrugged and said, "It doesn't matter. I don't even ask anymore." Then he put the trophy at the bottom of his bag, under his lunchbox.
What I did next: I took a photo of him with the trophy and told him how proud I was of his closing argument. With his agreement, I called his mother to tell her about the win and asked gently whether someone from home could come to the award function next month. She said she would make sure of it.

qa.q: Where had Dhruv saved a seat?
qa.a: In the second row, with his bag.

qa.q: What does Dhruv putting the trophy under his lunchbox suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Dhruv felt hurt and let down, burying his pride because the person he wanted to see it didn't come.

qa.q: What did Noor do after the final?
qa.a: Took a photo with the trophy, praised the closing argument, and with Dhruv's agreement called his mother about the award function next month.

qa.q: How might Dhruv's father feel hearing about the empty seat?
qa.a: His father might feel guilty and sad on learning Dhruv saved a seat and has stopped asking, if he realises what the missed events mean.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose father keeps missing promised events coming to believe he is not a priority and stopping asking, as seen by his coach.
